segments.text: Engineers start a new device with a paragraph and a few limits. Hardware Scientist turns it into an engineered concept: a picture you can trust, every number with its calculation, and a plan to make it. It is a design team built only from Meta models.

Expert agents work the problem on one shared whiteboard. An evaluator writes a critique. On a reject, the critique becomes a gradient that rewrites the team's own prompt. A picture loop then draws the design and checks every part, and lessons carry to the next problem.

Now the full architecture. The engineer gives only the what. In stage A, four experts and a chief designer search, calculate, simulate and sketch. The evaluator's written review is the loss. On a fail, the manager's two-step gradient rewrites only the guilty sections of the master prompt, and the meeting continues. Stage B draws the design.

A real step, from a lunar excavator. The evaluator rejected the first meeting: stowing was shown only as a volume, and tipping used placeholder masses. The output gradient says what must change; the prompt gradient finds the instruction that let it through, and the manager rewrites that rule. On the same board, the evaluator re-checks that issue first: 0.90 by 0.40 by 0.42 metres, met. This is TextGrad, applied to a whole team.
The whiteboard never resets. Across two meetings it grows from thirty-four sources and twelve calculations to sixty-eight and forty-four, with sketches pinned beside the numbers.

The picture loop. A code sketch fixes the geometry, Muse Image renders, SAM 3 masks every part, and a critic asks: is the render faithful to the sketch, and does it reveal a design flaw? A wrong part gets a local fix, kept only if nothing gets worse. A design flaw goes back to the council.

Our best result: a robot fingertip in the spirit of Meta's Digit 360. SAM finds the skin, pillars, flex circuit, core and cable; markers sit on each part's own pixels, and the scale comes from a hand. The figure shows how it works, how it is measured, and how it is made.
The same system designed an excavator, a turbine, a stair-climbing hand truck, a solar cold room and a footbridge damper.

How good is it? Two blind judges audited all six problems against one Meta prompt, re-deriving every number first. Honestly, it is a tie on average, about twenty-six of forty each. Hardware Scientist is more consistent, with better-supported numbers and fewer picture mistakes, and was preferred in seven of twelve verdicts. Its making plans are weaker: our next target.
On Meta's open-weights Muse Spark and SAM 3, the same loops run in half the time. Scores are lower for now, but the designs are still original.
Hardware Scientist builds on TextGrad, symbolic learning, Trace and context engineering. The engineer gives the what. Hardware Scientist works out the how, and shows its proof.
